blocks.content: kubectl edit opens a live object directly in your default text editor, saving applies the change immediately, a genuinely convenient, and genuinely risky, way to make quick, one-off changes.
edit pulls the object's current definition and opens it in your configured editor, letting you change it interactively, directly, rather than editing a separate manifest file first.

blocks.alt: The actual, live object, opened directly for interactive editing

blocks.content: The moment you save and close the editor, the change takes effect right away, there is no separate "apply" step, saving the file is the apply step.

blocks.alt: No separate confirmation step, saving the file is the action itself

blocks.content: 3. The Real Risk: Bypassing Version Control
blocks.text: 3. The Real Risk: Bypassing Version Control

blocks.content: This is the genuine downside worth understanding, an edit made this way exists only in the cluster, it never touches a tracked manifest file at all, the next time someone applies the original (now out of date) manifest, this live change is silently overwritten.

blocks.alt: A change that exists only in the cluster, invisible to version control entirely

blocks.content: 4. When It Is a Reasonable Choice
blocks.text: 4. When It Is a Reasonable Choice

blocks.content: For a genuine, urgent, one-off fix, bumping a replica count during an incident, for instance, edit is a reasonable, fast tool, just remember to reflect the change back into the tracked manifest afterward, so it does not get silently lost later.

blocks.alt: A fast fix for a genuine emergency, followed up by updating the real, tracked manifest

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl edit opens a live object directly for interactive editing, saving applies the change immediately, with no separate confirmation step.
Its real risk is bypassing version control entirely, a change made this way can be silently overwritten the next time someone applies the original manifest.
